lessons.title: Switching Rules for Salaried Employees vs Business and Professional Income

children.text: A salaried employee in Hyderabad and a doctor running her own clinic in Pune can face the same slabs and the same deductions, yet play by very different switching rules. One can hop between regimes every single year. The other gets essentially one round trip. Which group you fall into is decided by one question: do you have any business or professional income?

body.text: No business income: pick your regime fresh every year, as long as you file on time. Any business or professional income: you can leave the new regime, come back once, and then you are locked in.

markDefs.definition: Income from carrying on a trade, business, profession or vocation, including freelancing, consulting, medical or legal practice, trading in futures and options, intraday trading, and a partner's salary, bonus or interest from a partnership firm.

children.text: The stricter rules apply if you have any
in the year, however small, and even if most of your income is salary. The regime rules sit in Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act).

body.title: Sort the Income
body.question: Rajiv is a salaried manager at a Chandigarh bank. Which one of these extra incomes would move him into the stricter business-income switching rules?
options: ₹3,00,000 of rent from a flat in Mohali
₹1,20,000 of long-term gains from selling HDFC Bank shares
₹40,000 of profit from trading Bank Nifty options
₹85,000 of interest on SBI fixed deposits
body.explanation: F&O trading profit is business income, even when it is small and part-time. Rent, capital gains and FD interest are not, so on their own they leave Rajiv free to choose his regime every year.

children.text: Rule 1: No Business Income, Choose Each Year in Your Return

If your income comes only from salary, pension, house property, capital gains and other sources, the new regime applies by default and you can opt for the old regime simply by selecting it in your income tax return. Next year you can switch back, and the year after you can switch again. There is no separate form and no limit on the number of switches. The only condition is timing.

body.label: Deadline to choose the old regime (no business income)
body.value: The original return due date, usually 31 July
body.context: The option must be exercised in a return filed on or before the due date. Miss it, and the new regime applies automatically.

body.text: The belated return trap. If you file after the due date, you cannot opt for the old regime for that year, no matter how much it would have saved. You are taxed under the new regime, and on top of that you pay a late filing fee and interest on any unpaid tax. For anyone whose calculation favours the old regime, filing on time is worth real money.

body.caption: Pallavi, ₹40 Lakh Salary, Old Regime Saves ₹67,860 (Tax Year 2026-27)

cells: Nil if TDS covered her tax
Charged from August on the ₹67,860 gap

body.title: Remember the Condition
body.textWithBlank: A salaried taxpayer with no business income can choose the old regime only in a return filed on or before the ___ date.
body.explanation: The old regime option for non-business taxpayers must be exercised in a return filed by the original due date. A belated return is taxed under the new regime.

children.text: Rule 2: Business Income, One Exit and One Return

If you have business or professional income, choosing the old regime is not a tick box in your return. You must file a separate option form on the e-filing portal before the return due date (traditionally Form 10-IEA), and quote its acknowledgement number in your return. Once you opt out, you stay in the old regime every year until you withdraw. You can withdraw and move back to the new regime only once. After that, you can never opt out again for as long as you have business income.

body.title: Count the Switches
body.prompt: A freelance chartered accountant has already opted out of the new regime once and later withdrawn back into it. She still has professional income. How many more times can she opt for the old regime?
body.explanation: None. Having used her one withdrawal back to the new regime, she cannot opt out again while she continues to have business or professional income.

body.text: The lock is tied to having business income, not to your identity. If a person who used up their switch later stops all business and professional activity, for example a consultant who takes a full-time salaried job and stops freelancing, the yearly choice under Rule 1 becomes available again.

columns.label: No business or professional income
points: Choose old or new every year
Choice made directly in the return
Must file by the original due date to choose old
Declaration to employer affects only TDS

columns.label: Has business or professional income
points: Opt out once by filing an option form before the due date
Can return to the new regime only once
Then locked into the new regime while business income continues
Choice should be treated as a multi-year decision

body.title: How the option form has worked on the e-filing portal

children.text: Log in to the income tax e-filing portal with your PAN.
Go to e-File, then Income Tax Forms, and select the regime option form for the relevant year.
Confirm that you have business or professional income, and choose to opt out of or withdraw from the new regime.
Verify with Aadhaar OTP before the return due date and save the acknowledgement number.
Quote the acknowledgement number and date in your ITR-3 or ITR-4.

content.text: Form names and portal menus may change under the Income-tax Act, 2025 and its Rules. Check the current form on the e-filing portal for your tax year.

children.text: The biggest surprise for salaried Indians is that a small side hustle changes their rulebook. A few F&O trades on Zerodha, a weekend freelance project billed through Upwork, or a monetised Instagram page all create business or professional income. From that year on, the flexible yearly choice is gone, and every regime switch becomes a scarce resource.

body.title: Aakash Starts Freelancing
body.scenario: Aakash is a salaried UI designer in Bengaluru on ₹16 lakh and has always chosen his regime at filing time. In tax year 2026-27 he starts designing logos for small businesses and earns ₹2 lakh of freelance fees. His old regime benefits are ₹6,60,000 this year because of high rent, and his full comparison including the freelance fees shows the old regime only slightly ahead, but he expects to buy a home and stop renting within two years.
body.prompt: What changes for Aakash, and should he opt out of the new regime this year?
body.modelAnswer: His freelance fees are professional income, so the stricter rules now apply. Choosing the old regime is no longer a yearly tick box. He would need to file the option form before the due date, and he could come back to the new regime only once. His old regime advantage this year is marginal, just above breakeven, and his rent-driven HRA is likely to disappear within two years. If he opts out now, he will probably need to use his one withdrawal soon after he buys a home, and then be locked into the new regime for as long as he freelances. Given the thin margin, staying in the new regime and keeping his switch unused is a reasonable choice. Whatever he decides, he should rerun the full comparison every year, since freelance income added to his salary shifts his breakeven.

body.title: Pick the Right Switching Strategy
steps: List every income source for the year and check whether any is business or professional income
If none, run the comparison each year and file by the due date to keep the old regime option
If you have business income, treat opting out as a multi-year decision and project the next 3 to 5 years
If you opt out, file the option form before the due date and keep the acknowledgement number
Before withdrawing back to the new regime, remember it is your only return ticket
Set a calendar reminder for 15 July to file on time

points: The switching rules depend on one thing: whether you have any business or professional income in the year.
Without business income, you can choose the old or new regime every year directly in your return.
That choice is only available in a return filed by the original due date; a belated return is taxed under the new regime.
With business income, you must file an option form before the due date to leave the new regime.
You can return to the new regime only once, after which you cannot opt out again while business income continues.
Side income such as F&O trading or freelancing moves salaried taxpayers into the stricter rules.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Switching rules are described as they operated under Section 115BAC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and are expected to continue under Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025; confirm the current provisions, forms and deadlines for your tax year. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
